transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-25
Time: 15:00 - 15:47 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Malik (Redwood AE), Carlos Nguyen (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (CTO, Lodestar), Maya Chen (Lead ML Eng, Lodestar), Tom Reynolds (Infra, Lodestar)

Summary:
Quick recap of last week's throughput anomaly, compare current week latency/throughput vs Lodestar incumbent, discuss routing + quantization tweaks, agree next steps for expanded run and security follow-up.

Topics:
- p95/p99 latency deltas vs incumbent
- sustained throughput at 90% slot utilization
- KV cash (KV cache) and prefix reuse impact
- VPC peering and egress patterns
- SOC2/KMS questions for Private deployment

Action items (auto): see metadata action_items list

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha Malik: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We got about 45 minutes, we'll run through the lab numbers first, then routing/quant, and leave 10 minutes for security and next steps. Rajiv, Maya, Tom from Lodestar - thanks for making time.
[00:22] Rajiv Patel: Yeah thanks Aisha, we wanted to focus today on the latency gap we saw last Friday. We ran your suggested quant profile but saw p95 bounce up in the mid-300s intermittently, which is close to the incumbent.
[01:05] Carlos Nguyen: Right, useful to frame the runs: the set we looked at this week were the 2048-token prompt set, mixed batch pattern (mostly single-user queries with occasional 8-user bursts). Our baseline (Redwood hosted fastpath) numbers: median token latency ~45ms per token, p95 generation latency for the end-to-end request ~210ms. The incumbent you sent over had p95 ~340ms in your logs for the same sample.
[01:42] Maya Chen: The 340 number is what operations reported; but when we pushed steady load the incumbent had better throughput at peak, so part of our worry is tails under sustained load.
[02:10] Aisha Malik: Totally makes sense. Carlos, can you walk through what we changed in the quant and routing this sprint?
[02:25] Carlos Nguyen: Sure. We applied the mixed-precision quant profile Q-M3, which trades a little FP fidelity for faster matmuls. We also enabled prefix-sharing for repeated system prompts and increased the continuous batch window from 8ms to 12ms to allow slightly larger micro-batches. That yielded an average token-cost drop and improved throughput, but it can push p95 out a bit if KV cash hits are low or if the traffic is very bursty.
[03:10] Tom Reynolds: "KV cash" - just to be clear, that's KV cache, right? The transcript earlier in our tools calls it 'cash' sometimes.
[03:19] Carlos Nguyen: Yeah, sorry, KV cache. My bad, autocorrect.
[03:24] Rajiv Patel: The Friday anomaly - we saw a 3x jump in p99 for about 8 minutes. We traced it to a region fallback event in your logs. Was that due to routing policy?
[03:42] Carlos Nguyen: Good catch. There was an automated region fallback in the middle of that run — policy pushed some requests to a warm fallback pool with slightly different kernel selection; that can create a transient tail. We've updated the fallback threshold but for the run we didn't have the updated config.
[04:05] Maya Chen: Is the fallback because of slot saturation or a probe flapping?
[04:12] Carlos Nguyen: It was slot saturation on that cluster. Two things we discussed: 1) dedicated extra slots (we can provision) and 2) adjust the fallback threshold to prefer graceful queueing before cross-region spill.
[04:34] Aisha Malik: From a cost/resiliency trade-off, Lodestar wanted to test Redwood's hosted path vs a reserved dedicated pool. We measured both this week — can we summarize the numbers?
[04:46] Carlos Nguyen: Hosted fastpath (the one we mostly used) at 80% device utilization had sustained throughput ~520 tokens/s per slot for your model variant. Dedicated pool with conservative autoscale gave about 650 tokens/s at 90% utilization, but you pay reservation overhead. In your previous incumbent runs, they were getting 580 tokens/s sustained but with higher p95 times. So Redwood's dedicated option gave higher throughput in our lab, but requires commitment.
[05:30] Rajiv Patel: Those figures look good. The bigger worry is the latency tail during your fallback. If we can't guarantee tail behavior, it's hard for product to sign off.
[05:45] Carlos Nguyen: Understood. Two mitigations: bump the per-customer reserved burst capacity so spiky traffic doesn't trigger fallback, or tune routing to prefer local queue depth thresholds. Both are config changes we can push quickly for your pilot.
[06:10] Maya Chen: Also curious about tokenization differences. The incumbent uses a different tokenizer implementation which changes token counts on a subset of prompts; that could skew latency. Did you normalize tokenization for the side-by-side tests?
[06:25] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we used the same tokenizer binary your team submitted; small mismatch earlier was due to lib differences but we aligned them for the runs in the table we shared.
[06:40] Speaker 1: (inaudible) 
[06:50] Aisha Malik: Great. On quant: Rajiv asked if the Q-M3 profile might change hallucination rates or degrade quality. Carlos?
[07:00] Carlos Nguyen: We ran the quick eval suite — rouge/bleu-ish style checks and some semantic consistency sampling. Q-M3 increased minor token-level diffs in ~2% of examples but we didn't surface increased factual hallucinations in the set we ran. Caveat: larger production prompt sets could reveal more regressions, so we recommend a short prompt-set eval tied to your SLOs before flipping in production.
[07:37] Maya Chen: We'll run our full eval against Q-M3 and Q-M2 (less aggressive) and send results.
[07:47] Rajiv Patel: On security: we need KMS integration details and SOC2 audit artifacts. We're also checking for SSO/SAML integration and RBAC for model-level keys.
[07:58] Aisha Malik: We'll schedule a security deep-dive. Carlos, do we have the KMS docs link?
[08:06] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, I've got the internal doc link — I'm going to paste it in the notes. It's a short read: KMS integration patterns, HSM option for Private, and envelope encryption. Also, there is a SOC2 snapshot we can share under NDA.
[08:25] Tom Reynolds: For our compliance team, any mention of audit logs retention and per-request payload redaction?
[08:34] Carlos Nguyen: Audit logs are available, retention is configurable as an add-on. Payload redaction can be configured at the ingestion hook to strip PII before it hits logs. We'll put the specifics in the security follow-up.
[08:50] Rajiv Patel: Back to perf — can you walk through the p95 time-series for the 20k steady run? We saw periodic spikes every ~7 minutes.
[08:58] Carlos Nguyen: We pulled the time-series. The 7-minute spikes correlated with background checkpoint compaction jobs on the node pool in that run — compaction briefly took CPU cycles and impacted kernel scheduling. We've adjusted compaction windows to the 03:00 maintenance window but in your lab run the compaction collided with a high-latency period.
[09:30] Maya Chen: Is that an ops tuning thing we can coordinate so production runs don't overlap with GC/compaction?
[09:36] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — schedule maintenance windows and we'll avoid heavy compaction during your large runs. Also, for long tails we can enable soft preemption for background ops.
[09:50] Rajiv Patel: Another point: network egress patterns. We saw a small number of retries due to transient packet drops on the peered VPC path in your logs. Tom, any notes?
[10:02] Tom Reynolds: We are already looking at VPC peering path MTU and keepalives. We'll share the current peering diagram.
[10:10] Aisha Malik: Perfect. Now, any changes to the test plan for next week? Carlos?
[10:18] Carlos Nguyen: For the follow-up run, we propose: 1) enable updated fallback threshold, 2) provision 2 extra dedicated slots for 30 minutes during the 20k steady run, 3) run both Q-M2 and Q-M3 profiles back-to-back, 4) collect full traces and system metrics. We'll drop a config gist.
[10:40] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll also pass in our larger prompt set and ramp to 25k users if results are stable.
[10:50] Rajiv Patel: On pricing: if we move to dedicated, can we get a short-term reservation for the rest of the pilot window without the full annual commit?
[10:59] Aisha Malik: Yes — we can do a monthly reserved block for pilots. I'll send a pricing addendum.
[11:08] Rajiv Patel: Great.
[11:12] Speaker 2 (inaudible):
[11:20] Tom Reynolds: One more infra question — network egress costs. Do you have an estimator for egress vs incumbent?
[11:28] Carlos Nguyen: We do. It's in the pricing sheet I'll attach. Generally similar; depends on region egress and whether you use Private with peering.
[11:40] Maya Chen: Ok, let's talk about acceptance criteria. For product sign-off we need p95 <= 300ms and p99 <= 600ms for our 2048 prompt set at 20k steady concurrency. Also quality regressions < 1% on our eval.
[11:58] Aisha Malik: That is clear. We'll aim for a run that demonstrates p95 <= 300ms. If hitting tails, we'll show mitigation steps and metrics.
[12:10] Rajiv Patel: Can we get a short video or walkthrough of the tracing UI you use for these runs? Our devs found your tracing helpful in the last session.
[12:20] Carlos Nguyen: I'll record a 8-minute walkthrough and drop it in the shared drive.
[12:28] Aisha Malik: Ok, final five minutes - recap and owners.
[12:33] Aisha Malik: Recap: Redwood to push routing + quant config gist, provision 2 extra slots during next run, share KMS/SOC2 docs under NDA, send pricing addendum for monthly reserved block; Lodestar to run expanded loadtest (20-25k) and share eval results and traffic distribution; schedule security deep-dive.
[12:55] Rajiv Patel: Yep, all good. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[13:02] Carlos Nguyen: No blockers. We'll get the configs out today/tomorrow.
[13:10] Maya Chen: We'll aim to run the expanded test on Monday/Tuesday next week and upload artifacts.
[13:18] Aisha Malik: Great — I'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep-dive. Thanks everyone.
[13:25] (meeting ends)
